chapter.title: The pyScaler program
chapter.para: pyScaler is a new scaler display program that is part of the FRIB initiative to decouple FRIB/NSCLDAQ from Tcl/Tk. pyScaler was written in Pythion3 using the Qt graphical user interface toolkit. The visual display of pyScaler is quite similar to the ScalerDisplay program. See also the manpage for

At the top of the window, run state and run information (title, run number, time into the run) are displayed. Below that is a tabbed notebook of scaler counter lines. At the bottom of the window are optional strip charts showing the time evolution of selected scaler rates and ratios.

Where the pyScaler application differs from the ScalerDisplay is the struture of the configuration file. The ScalerDisplay used a Tcl script with extended commands to define scalers and their sources, which were identified by sourcde id. This option is not available in Python. pyScaler uses Tom's Obvious Minimal Language, or TOML, as it's usually abbreviated. For information about what TOML looks like, see: .
For this discussion, it's only important to know that TOML files are divided into sections. Each section has a name inside of square brackets. For example:
Is a section named datasource.raw1. pyScaler uses the following sections:

listitem.para: Defines the characteristic of a source of data for pyScaler. The program can accept data from more than one data source. Data sources have names, the name of the data source is the text following the period. For example: [datasourcde.focal-plane] is a section that defines a data source named focal-plane

Defines a page of scalers. The page appears as a tab in the tabbed notebook of counters. Pages have names as well, which appear on their tabl of the tabbed notebook e.g. [pages.live-times] is a page named live-times and will generate a tab labeled with the text live-times.
Defines the strip charts to display on the bottom section of the display.
Defines any alamr levels to apply to scalers.
Describes the colors of the various alarm levels.

chapter.para: Each section has a specific set of key/value pairs. The remaining sections in this chapter describe each section and the keyword/value pairs that are recognized.

note.title: NOTE
note.para: The TOML parser used by pyScaler does not know anything about the semantics of the file. It only understands and parses proper syntax. pyScaler performs some sanity checks and outputs warnings to stderr for any issues it detects, however these are not exhaustive.

section.title: [datasource.source-name]
section.para: These sections define the sources from which the pyScaler takes data and the scalers that each data source provides. pyScaler can support data from any FRIB/NSCLDAQ data format 10.0 and greater.
The key/value pairs supported by the datasource sections are:

listitem.para: The value of this key is a string that is the URL of the ring buffer from which data will be taken. For example; url='tcp://spdaq30.frib.msu.edu/raw'. This key is mandatory and omitting it will generate a warning.

The value of this optional key is an integer that is the major version of the data format expected from the source. If pyScaler sees a RING_FORMAT item that differs from this it transparently changes the frormat to the version in that item. For example; version=12. If this key is omitted, the source format defaults to 12.

The value of this key is an array of scaler names. These names are assigned to items in the scaler item in the order in which they occur in the array. For example: scalers=['triggers.live', 'triggers'] says the source will provide two scalers that are, in order triggers.live and triggers
The value of this optional key is a boolean. Note that in toml booleans are specified by one of two values: true or false. All lower case and not quoted See, the example.

If the value is true (the default if not specified), scalers from the source are assumed to be cleared as the are read, providing incrmeental counts over the counting interval. If false the scalers are assumed to count continuously, cleared only at the beginnig of the run. pyScaler assumes all scalers are 32 bits. If a subsequent count value in a nonicremental channel is less than the previous count value, a single overflow of the scaler is assumed to have occured and is properly accounted for.

section.para: Here is an example of a complete data source section for a data source named raw

example.title: pyScaler data source section
example.programlisting: [datasource.example] url='tcp://spdaq30/raw' version=12 scalers=['triggers.live', 'triggers', 'sin1', 'sin2', 'sin3', 'sin4', 'sin5', 'sin6', 'sin7', 'sin8', 'sin9', 'sin10'] incremental=false # Scalers count continuously.

section.para: The names in the scalers array are called unqualified names. The fully qualified name of a scaler is preceded by the data source name followed by a period. For example, the fully qualified name of triggers.live is example.triggers.live. Keep this in mind when we describe the contents of the pages sections.

section.title: [pages.pagename]
section.para: The purpose of a pages section is to describe the contents of a tab in the tabbed notebook of counters. The pagename part of the pages section is displayed on the tab of the tabbed notebook. title key takes a string value and displays that title string at the top of the page.
The remaining keys of a pages section are of the form linen where n is an integer and specifies the line of the page being described.
The contents of linen keys are an inline table. See for a description of inline tables. For our purposes, an inline table is a set of key/value pairs wrapped in curly brackets.
Two keys are accepted in the linen keys. Both are required:

listitem.para: Describes the type of line. The valid line types are single which displays a single scaler and its rates. pair which displays a pair of scalers and their rates. nand ratio which displays a pair of scalers, and their rates as well as their intantaneous ratio and ratio of rates. For example line1={type='single', ....}

Is an array containing one or two (depending on the type) of fully qualified scaler names to display on the line. For exmaple, using the data source desribed in the previous section: line1={type='ratio', scalers=['example.triggers.live', 'example.triggers']} Note how the data source name is used to fully qualify the scaler names. This allows for scalers with identical names from different data sources. pyScaler will display the fully qualified scaler names.

example.title: Example pyScaler pages section

note.title: NOTE
note.para: If a line number is omitted, as shown in the example above where we go from line2 to line4, skipping line3, the skipped line will be empty. This can help you make the display of counters more readable.

section.title: [graph]
section.para: If this optional section is present, a stripchart will be displayed at the bottom of the pyScaler display. This section describes what is charted. There are two sorts of plots that can be made, individual plots provide a strip chart of the rates of individual scalers. ratios plots provide a stripchart of ratios of rates. The value of each of these keys is an array which allows you to have several lines on the plots.
As with the pages sections, scaler names must be fully qualified.
Two other keys can optionally be specified:

listitem.para: The value of this is the integer number of seconds that will be shown in the plots. As points are added, the plot is shifted to display the most recent time interval described by this. If not supplied, this defaults to 3600 or one hour. Note that the controls on the display allow you to move the displayed window, for a while.

For very long runs, the number of points plotted can grow without bounds until the display runs out of virtual memory in which to hold them. If specified, this describes a threshold number of points above which the points prior to the window are decimated. Currently, the decimation factor is hard-coded to 2. That is when decimation is done, every other data point before the window is deleted. Bit by bit, older data will be retained with lower and lower time resolution. Note that if not supplied, this defaults to 100000 which, at typical scaler rates of 2 seconds is somewhat more than 2 days of data taking.

section.para: The example plots the rate of accepted triggers and the ratio of live triggers to triggers. The rate of the sin1 scaler from the example data source is also plotted. Note how the ratios keyword takes an array of arrays. The optional window keyword allows you to override the default display window of the last hour of data by supplying a new display window in seconds. The optiona trim_to allows you to specify the decimation threshold which defaults to 100000.

Decimation prevents the data saved from growing without bound. Once the number of points in any data series grows above the trim_to decimation threshold, data before the display window are decimated by removing every other data point. The default of 100,000 means that at typical scaler readout rates of once every 2 seconds, over 2 days of data are saved before decimation is triggered. This is needed because the controls on the plot window allow scrollling the data prior to the window.

section.title: [output]
section.para: At the end of the run, the scaler display writes several files. The path keyword, which takes a string argument, allows you tot specify the directory in which those files are written. If not specified, the oputut directory defaults to the current working directory of the pyScaler.
The files written have names like runnnnn where nnnn is the run number, and varying extension depending on what's written in the file:

listitem.para: Contains a human readable report of scaler totals and average rates.

Is a file that is machine readable (e.g. can be imported in to Excel). It consists of a header line that contains, in order, the run number, title, start time and end time as well as the duration. Subsequent lines contain the full scaler name, its total counts, its average rate and standard deviation from the average.
This file is only written if strip charts are graphed. In that case, it is the plot at the end of the run in PNG format. One way to view these files is with the xdg-open command

section.title: [alarms]
section.para: You can set upper and lower limit alarms on the rates of scalers. This section describes the alarm limits. See, as well
A line in the [alarms] has as a key the fully qualified name of a scaler. The value of the line is an inline array with one or more of the following keys:

listitem.para: The value of this an integer. When the rate of this scaler is above this value, it is said to be in the high alarm state and that's indicated on the display by colorizing the value, it's total and rates. The tab of the page is also colorized. See [alarmcolors] below.
The value of this is a integer. When the rate of this scaler is below this value, it is said to be in the low alarm state and is colorized as is the tab of the page containing the alarmed scaler

section.title: [alarmcolors]
section.para: This section describes the colors used to indicate both that scalers are in an alarm state and that tabs have scalers in the alarmed state. Each of the keys has as a values the name of a color taken from the predefined Qt color list. The recognized keys are:

listitem.para: The value of this key is the color used to indicate a scaler is in the low alarm state. It also is used to indicate a tab has scalers in the low alarm state but none in the high alarm state.
The value of this key is the color used to indicates a scaler is in the high alarm state. It is also used to indicate a tab has scalers in the high alarm state but not the low alarm state.
The value of this key is a color used to indicate a tab has scalers in both the high and low alarm states.
The value of this key is a color used to indicate both that a scaler is not in an alarmed state and that a tab has no scalers in the alarmed state.

note.title: NOTE
note.para: If the [alarmcolors] section is omitted, or one of the keys is omitted, default colors are used. The example above, actually shows the default color choices.

refsect1.title: DESCRIPTION
refsect1.para: The pyScaler command provides a display of scaler totals, rates and seleted ratios of totals and rates at run-time. The config-file parameter is the path to a TOML configuration file. See CONFIGURATION FILE below. The configuration file describes to pyScaler where it gets scalers from and what to display.

The pyScaler command provies a window with three sections. The top section provides information about the run and run state. The middle section is a tabbed notebook providing live scaler totals, rates and totals. The bottom, optional section provides strip charts for selected scaler rates and ratios of scaler rates.

refsect1.title: CONFIGURATION FILE
refsect1.para: The pyScaler program is driven by a configuraiton file written in Tom's Obvious Minmal Language or TOML as it is usually abbreviated.
This section will annotate a simple, sample configuration file.

example.title: Sample pyScaler TOML configuration file

callout.para: Sections with names that begin with datasource. define ringbuffers that will be read by pyScaler and the scalers those ring buffers will provide. The part of the section name following the datasource. is the name of the datasource. You can specify as many data sources as you need.
The url key in the data source section specifies the URL of the ring buffer from which the program will accept data. The pyScaler program only takes in scaler items and run state change items.

The pyScaler program can accept data from any ringbuffer version of FRIB/NSCLDAQ. The version key specifies the major version of data expected on that data sourcde (in this case version 11.x). Note that the version value is an integer as the ring item format is fixed within a major version of FRIB/NSCLDAQ. If pyScaler receives a RING_FORMAT item on the data source, it will use that item to transparently change, if necessary, the data source format decoded. If this item is missing, 12 is used.

The value of the scalers key is an array of strings. The strings are the unqualified names of the scalers, in the order in which they will apppear in scaler items from the source. The scaler names are said to be fully qualified when the data source name is inclded as well, for example, in this data sourcde, the fully qualified name of name1 is raw2.name1. Note that duplicate unqualified names are allowed if they are in different sources.

Scalers from this source will count continuously. Note that scalers from raw2 are incremental because the incremental keyword is not given, and that is the default. You may explicitly tag the scalers from a data source as incremental by adding the key/value pair: incremental=true

For each page you want in the tabbed notebook of scaler counts, totals and ratios, you must have a pages.page-name section. The page-name part of the section name labels the tab of the page that section describes. Page names should be unique.
Page names must have titles. Titles are a string of text displayed at the top of the page.

The scaler lines on a page are described by a series of line line-no keys. The line_no part of that key is the number (tarting from 1) of the line of the display being described. Omitted line numbers are empty, as in the description of [pages.another] where line2 is omitted.

Two keys must appear in the table of key/value pairs in the line directives: type is the type of line. It can be one of single, pair or ratio. scalers is an array of fully qualified scaler names. for single lines, the array contains the name of the single scaler to display. For pair and ratio lines the array contains the pair of scalers to display. For ratio the first scaler is the numerator of the ratios.
The [graph] section is optional. It is only needed if you want pyScaler to display strip charts.
The individual keyword in the [graph] section lists the scalers whose rates you want plotted on the stip chart. Note the value is an array of fully qualified scaler names.

The ratios keyword on the [graph] section lists the pairs of scalers whose ratios of rats you want plotted. Note the value is an array of two element arrays of fully qualified scaler names. The first element of each array is the numerator name.

Scalers can low and high level alarms set on their rates. A scaler with a rate below its low alarm level is said to be in low alarm state and it is colorized with the lowalarm color. Salers with rates above their high alamr level are said to be in the high alarm state and are colorized with the highalarm color.

Furthermore, the tabs of pages with scalers in alamr state are colorized. If all alarms are the same level, they are colorized with the color of that alarm level. On the other hand, if alarms of both types are present, they are colorized with the bothalarms color.
This section is optional. You only need to provide it if you are specifying alarms.

The keywords of the [alarms] secion are fully qualified scaler names. Their values are an inline table with keys high and low to specify the high and low alarm thresholds respectively. It is legal to specify only one of those keywords, in which case, only that type of alarm is defined for that scaler.

The colors used to indicate alarms can be tailored. Any or all of the color keywords can be used to override the defaults. The color names must come from those in the predefined Qt color list. The example shows the actual default colors if eithyer [alarmcolors] is not specified or one of the keys is not provided in that section.

refsect1.title: FILES
refsect1.para: At the end of the run, pyScaler writes several files. Note that in the descriptions that follow, nnnn is the run number of the run that ended.

listitem.para: Provides a human readable summary of the average rates and totals. The format of this file should be obvious on inspection.

A file in comma separated field format that can be imported into programs (e.g. directly into Excel). The first line of the file provides the run number, ttle, start time, end time, and duration of the run. Subsequent lines provide the full name of a scaler, the total counts, average rate and standard deviation of counts from that average for each scaler.
This file is only written if you graph stripcharts. In that case, this file is a PNG image of the strip chart at the end of the run.
